baqt.value: Non-aggression pact after the Muslim attack on Dongola in 31/651-2; Makuria kept its independence and each side's subjects could travel and trade freely in the other's territory. It ended when Nubia's rulers became Muslim.

rating.note: Source reports both gains (agriculture, trade security) and harm (new taxation 'disrupted the economic life'); rating by the Historian.

rating_basis_en.value: The Turkish administration improved irrigation and crops and gave traders greater security (p.361), but extended the Egyptian taxation system to the Sudan, which 'inevitably disrupted the economic life of the people', collected by brutal means (p.362); Muhammad Ali's gold mining at Fazughli failed (p.361).

rating_basis_ar.value: حسّنت الإدارة التركية الري والمحاصيل ووفرت للتجار أمنًا أكبر (ص.361)، لكنها مدّت نظام الضرائب المصري إلى السودان فأربك حتمًا الحياة الاقتصادية للناس، وكانت الجباية بوسائل وحشية (ص.362)؛ وفشل تعدين الذهب في فازوغلي (ص.361).

economic_base.value: Kropáček says the usual picture of a flourishing Alodia rests mainly on Ibn Sulaym (from 975) and Abu Salih (early 13th c.), plus Muslim merchants' reports, 'for 'Alwa was a good market for the purchase of slaves'. Abu Salih describes the kingdom 'in full prosperity, with some 400 churches'. In its decline, Arab immigrants took control of pastures, and its human resources were 'probably already weakened by the slave trade' (GHA IV ch.16, p.406). No account of production or taxation was read. GHA III adds Ibn Salim al-Aswani's account, quoted by al-Maqrizi: Soba had magnificent buildings and gardens and 'churches overflowing with gold', and Alodia's king ruled 'a land that was far more fertile' than Makuria. Jakobielski stresses 'we know next to nothing of Alodia' (GHA III ch.8, p.196). Ibn Hawqal reports that pastoral peoples in Kordofan owed allegiance to the king of Makuria or of Alodia (p.199).

economic_base.value: Before 1860 a trading system grew up in the kingdom, which the reth (king) 'could no longer control' as foreigners came to dominate it. Kaka in northern Shillukland became the main slave market of the White Nile after 1854. Kate Petherick called the Shilluk 'an industrious people' who 'cultivated grain to a large extent'. One raid by Muhammad al-Khayr is recorded as taking 500 slaves and 12,000 head of cattle. Turco-Egyptian rule then imposed heavy cattle taxes, an annual tribute of £15,000 on the Shilluk and Jieng, and cotton grown with forced labour around Fashoda (5,000–6,000 ha by 1874) (GHA VI ch.14, pp.366–367).

economic_base.value: Kropáček calls the baqt 'a convenient formula for economic interdependence', observed for six centuries despite occasional raids (GHA IV ch.16, p.398). Muslim merchants could travel freely in Nubia, though settlement was usually tolerated only in the northern borderland (p.401). Black troops of Sudani origin, 'largely obtained from Mukurra and 'Alwa', were an important part of the Fatimid army (p.401). In the 7th–11th centuries Nubia imported grain, wine, linen and cloth under the bakt, plus glass from Egypt. It exported mainly slaves, with gold, ivory and skins also traded. Internal trade was by barter; Egyptian coin circulated only in the north, and a customs frontier at Upper Maks ('Akasha) separated the foreign-trade zone from the royal-controlled heartland (GHA III ch.8, p.207). Jakobielski suggests Kordofan and Darfur may have supplied the bakt slaves (p.199).

economic_base.value: For Sudan, the Condominium economy rested partly on Egyptian money. Because taxes in Sudan were light, Britain and Egypt agreed that Egypt would give Sudan financial aid and loans for development and the budget: Egypt's contribution to the Sudanese budget was about £E 2.8 million for 1899–1916, and Egyptian loans about £E 5.4 million for 1900–10 (GHA VII ch.17, pp.455–456). The Gezira cotton scheme, started in 1911 by the Sudan government and the private Sudan Plantations Syndicate to supply Britain's textile industry, made cotton 'the mainstay of the country's economy' (LOC1991_CONDO; GHA VII ch.17, p.455, which gives the 40/35/25 tenant/government/syndicate split and the Sennar Dam of 1925).

economic_base.value: The Zande developed high-yield farming that fed a dense population, about 40 per km² in the 1870s according to Schweinfurth, swelled by captives taken in the aristocracy's raids (GHA VI ch.12, p.300). In the 19th century, Sudanese traders built zaribas and fortified bases in Zande country and mixed state monopoly and private trade with armed force (p.306). Before 1800, Darfur took copper tribute near Hofrat en-Nahas, north of Zande lands (GHA V ch.7, p.199).

economic_base.value: Mecca was a commercial centre on the caravan route, and the pilgrimage brought profit (GHA III ch.2, p.33). The bakt allowed free travel and trade (ch.3, p.81). Arab merchants had a quarter in Dongola, and from the 8th century they settled in 'Aydhab, Badi' and Sawakin (p.82).

economic_base.value: From the Fatimids until the Portuguese, the Red Sea was the main route to India; Muslim merchants developed 'Aydhab and Sawakin, and Sawakin was probably Nubia's main outlet (GHA IV ch.16, pp.417–418). Baybars's tribute was 80 slaves, 300 camels and 30 kintars of ivory a year (p.418). Under the Funj, Sawakin was Sennar's main outlet by the 'Sudan Road' (GHA V ch.6, p.175; ch.7, p.181). The Hadariba traded slaves from Shendi for Indian goods, making Sawakin the main slave centre after Cairo and Massawa (ch.7, p.184). In the 19th century a railway from Suakin to Khartoum was planned (GHA VI ch.13, p.334).

economic_base.value: GHA V says Kordofan was disputed between the Fur and the Funj 'primarily for economic reasons', with the Musabba'at trying to consolidate their hold there (ch.7, p.187), and that Tayrab's campaign was 'probably' driven by a wish to curb the Musabba'at's 'attempt to establish a strong state in Kordofan and to control the trade routes, the sources of slaves and gold in southern Kordofan' (p.189). No source read describes how the Musabba'at economy itself worked. Holt & Daly note that rivalry over Kordofan, together with the Shilluk on the White Nile, made the direct caravan route from Kubayh to Sennar via El Obeid unsafe, so caravans went north from El Obeid to Shendi (HD2011, intro p.8). Holt & Daly do not name the Musaba'at; the link is the period and the region only.
